books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address, March 5, 1877

stimulus.text:
“The evils which afflict the Southern States can only be removed or remedied by the united and harmonious efforts of both races, actuated by motives of mutual sympathy and regard; and while in duty bound and fully determined to protect the rights of all by every constitutional means at the disposal of my Administration, I am sincerely anxious to use every legitimate influence in favor of honest and efficient local self-government as the true resource of those States for the promotion of the contentment and prosperity of their citizens.”

—President Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address, March 5, 1877
stimulus.source_note: Rutherford B. Hayes, Inaugural Address, March 5, 1877. Public domain (presidential address; text verified against the Miller Center transcript and Wikisource).

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Hayes also promised to “protect the rights of all by every constitutional means.” The tension in his address is best explained by the fact that

options.text: the Constitution gave the president no power over the states at all.
options.misconception: Background: the president could still use federal law and the courts; the limit was political will, not constitutional power.

options.text: Hayes had lost the popular vote and had no authority to act.
options.misconception: Background: Hayes was the lawful president; the problem was the bargain that had put him there.

options.text: Southern Democrats had promised to protect Black voting rights.
options.misconception: Background: the Redeemer governments did the opposite; they moved to limit Black voting.

options.text: his promise depended on the very federal power his bargain was giving up.

rationales.A: Background: the president could still use federal law and the courts; the limit was political will, not constitutional power.
rationales.B: Background: Hayes was the lawful president; the problem was the bargain that had put him there.
rationales.C: Background: the Redeemer governments did the opposite; they moved to limit Black voting.
rationales.D: Hayes pledged to guard Black rights, but the only tool strong enough to do it, federal troops and enforcement, was what he traded away for the presidency. The promise and the bargain pulled in opposite directions.
rationales.general:
1. Hayes makes two promises in one sentence: protect all rights, and favor local self-government.
2. Background: protecting Black rights in 1877 needed federal troops, marshals, and prosecutions.
3. Local self-government meant removing those very tools and trusting Southern governments instead.
4. So the address promises a result while giving up the means to reach it.
Remember: when a speech promises two things that need opposite actions, one of them is the real policy.
